subject: history_social
passage: For more than a century, the Olympic motto consisted of three Latin words, "Citius, Altius, Fortius," which Pierre de Coubertin proposed when the International Olympic Committee was founded in 1894. Coubertin had borrowed the phrase from his friend Henri Didon, a priest who used it as a motto for the athletes at his school. In English, the motto means ______ Higher, Stronger." In 2021, the committee added a fourth word, "Communiter," which means "Together."
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.why: The translation "Faster, Higher, Stronger" is the object of the verb "means," so no punctuation comes between "means" and the opening quotation mark. Inside the quotation, the three words of the motto are separated by commas, just as they are in the Latin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The quotation does not end after "Faster"; the closing quotation mark comes after "Stronger," so this mark is misplaced.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon can't come between the verb "means" and its object, the quoted translation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate simple words in a short list; the words of the motto are separated by commas.
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation separates "means" from its quoted object, and a comma separates the first two words of the motto.
